libraries.name: sqlite3
libraries.description: Store and query records in a local SQLite database.
libraries.snippet:
import sqlite3

with sqlite3.connect(":memory:") as database:
    database.execute("CREATE TABLE journeys (name TEXT, destination TEXT)")
    # Parameters keep user values separate from SQL commands.
    database.execute("INSERT INTO journeys VALUES (?, ?)", ("Rob Johnston", "Manchester"))
    for row in database.execute("SELECT name, destination FROM journeys"):
        print(row)
# Replace :memory: with a chosen database path to retain records.

libraries.name: datetime
libraries.description: Compare full departure dates and apply an inclusive time limit.
libraries.snippet:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

driver = datetime.strptime("08/10/2026 09:15", "%d/%m/%Y %H:%M")
rider = datetime.strptime("08/10/2026 09:00", "%d/%m/%Y %H:%M")
matches = abs(driver - rider) <= timedelta(minutes=15)
print(matches)
# Keep the date as well as the time when a journey can cross midnight.

libraries.name: Browser button
libraries.description: Create a visible browser button and count its clicks. Use this for the first interactive control on a web page; no third-party library is required.
libraries.install: Built into a modern web browser; document is unavailable in Node.js.
libraries.explanation: The DOM represents the browser page as objects. createElement creates a button; appendChild makes it visible. addEventListener connects a click to a callback. let stores a count that changes; const keeps the button binding fixed while allowing its properties to change.
libraries.usage:
1. Select JavaScript and add this snippet to an empty workbench.
2. Choose Check syntax, then Run code and confirm the reviewed code. DOM code opens in Web preview.
3. Click the button twice and compare its label with the expected result.
4. Add another event handler or a second control using different variable names. Keep the original button code.
libraries.expected_output: Initially: Click me. After the first click: Clicked 1 time(s). After the second: Clicked 2 time(s). The label changes only when clicked.

libraries.name: Python built-ins
libraries.description: Create a list of numbers, calculate its total and display the result using Python's built-in sum and print functions.
libraries.install: Python 3; no extra packages. Save as starter.py and run python starter.py.
libraries.snippet:
numbers = [2, 4, 6]
total = sum(numbers)
print(f"Total: {total}")
libraries.explanation: The list stores three integers. sum adds them and returns 12. The assignment keeps that result in total; the f-string inserts it into a readable message, and print displays that message. Use this pattern to calculate a summary from several values.

libraries.name: JavaScript Array and console
libraries.description: Add numeric array values with reduce and show the result with console.log. Runs in Node.js or a browser console without external packages.
libraries.install: Node.js; save as starter.js and run node starter.js. A browser console also supports this example.
libraries.explanation: const creates bindings for the array and calculated total. reduce calls the arrow function with the running sum and each value, starting from 0. The template literal inserts total into the output. This is similar to Python sum(numbers), but JavaScript uses an array method and an explicit accumulator callback.

libraries.name: C++ iostream and numeric
libraries.description: Use the C++ standard library to calculate an array total and display it. No third-party library is required.
libraries.install: A C++ compiler; g++ starter.cpp -o starter, then run the produced executable.
libraries.explanation: iostream declares the standard output stream; numeric declares accumulate. main is the executable entry point. The integer array contains three values; numbers and numbers + 3 mark the beginning and one-past-the-end of its range. accumulate adds that range starting from 0. cout streams the label and result to the console. Unlike Python, this source must be compiled and its types and headers checked before execution.

libraries.name: C stdio.h
libraries.description: Calculate an integer total and print it with the C standard input/output library.
libraries.install: A C99-or-later compiler; gcc -std=c99 starter.c -o starter, then run the produced executable.
libraries.explanation: stdio.h declares printf. main starts the program and returns a status code. int explicitly selects integer storage. The loop visits indexes 0, 1 and 2, adding each array element to total. printf uses %d as the placeholder for that integer and a newline to finish the output line. Python could express the calculation as sum(numbers); C requires declared types and explicit loop or library operations, and braces delimit the loop body.

libraries.name: C string.h
libraries.description: Use strlen to count bytes before the terminating null in a C string. This is not a Unicode character counter.
libraries.install: A C compiler; gcc starter.c -o starter, then run the produced executable.
libraries.explanation: The character array stores Hello followed by a terminating null byte. string.h declares strlen, which counts bytes up to that terminator; it returns size_t, printed using %zu. const prevents changes to this array through its declared name. Python len on a string counts Unicode code points, so its result is not always interchangeable with C strlen on encoded bytes.

libraries.name: CMake built-in list operations
libraries.description: Use a CMake list, foreach and math(EXPR) to calculate a total. Run this as a CMake script; it does not compile C or C++ source.
libraries.install: CMake 3.16 or later; save as starter.cmake and run cmake -P starter.cmake.
libraries.snippet:
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.16)
set(numbers 2 4 6)
set(total 0)
foreach(value IN LISTS numbers)
    math(EXPR total "${total} + ${value}")
endforeach()
message(STATUS "Total: ${total}")
